newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan investment in China at turning point.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan investment in China at turning point.

text.p: Japanese companies looking to make money in China are concerned more with taxation and tariff policies than territorial disputes over tiny islands.

Business experts say Beijing's changing and sometimes seemingly fickle policies toward foreign investors have made Japanese companies cautious. But they add that the lure of the huge potential market on Japan's Asian doorstep will probably grow.

Japanese direct investment in China "is at a turning point," said Kazuhiro Takeda, an official at the Japan-China Association on Economy and Trade, which recently took a mission of top executives from 50 Japanese companies to China.

"Until now, most Japanese investment in China was aimed at reducing costs to make competitive exports. Now companies are considering how to boost production capacity in China to cultivate China's domestic market, which will open gradually over the next three to five years," Takeda said.
The Japanese business delegation arrived in China last month in the midst of a row between Tokyo and Beijing over a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea.

The dispute fuelled anti-Japanese sentiment among nationalists in China, Taiwan and Hong Kong and forced Beijing to walk a fine line between protecting ties with its vital neighbour and retaining its nationalist credentials.

The Japanese group, in China partly to present a list of sought-after changes that Japanese firms say would improve the foreign investment environment, got an unwelcome reminder that diplomatic rows can creep into business matters.

The executives got a clear message to take back home -- China is trying to keep calm and wants Japan to take a more considered approach, said Ryusuke Ikegami, an official at the Japan-China Investment Promotion Organisation.
The territorial row over the islands, which are claimed by China, Japan and Taiwan, has been giving diplomats a headache, and business would certainly like to see calm prevail.
JAPANESE BUSINESS CONCERNED AT CHANGES IN CHINESE POLICY
But Japanese businesses are mostly focusing on the repercussions of China's continuing whittling away of policies that promoted foreign investment with preferential treatment.
Such policies, which helped boost foreign ventures to the point where they account for nearly 40 percent of China's trade, have been undergoing revision for the past two years.

In April, for example, China abolished tariff exemptions on imports of capital goods and raw materials for foreign ventures. The move was in tandem with sweeping tariff cuts that appeared mostly to benefit Chinese firms and consumers.
Japanese firms already in China are resigned to the changing policy but unhappy with the way its implementation is being handled, Japan-China business experts say.
"China has shifted its policy to reduce preferential treatment for foreign firms and its manner of doing so has not been stable," Ikegami said.
High on the Japanese firms' list of headaches has been Beijing's failure to deliver promised tax rebates for exports. Arbitrary fees imposed by local authorities are another unwelcome cost.
A member of last month's business mission said Chinese officials promised to study their suggestions for improving the investment climate. But he expressed doubts about how quickly they would act.

"Their response was very positive, but there are some aspects that will take time," said Atsuhiko Umeda, executive managing director of the Japan-China Association on Economy and Trade. "They are in a tight fiscal situation and tax revenues are low, so it will not be so easy to remedy the tax problem."

Japanese business also wants Beijing to move faster to remove discriminatory restrictions on foreign firms to make up for the loss of preferential treatment. "There isn't much progress in that direction," Ikegami said.
TIGHT MONETARY POLICY DAMPENS APPETITE FOR INVESTMENT

Prospects that Beijing will keep its monetary policy tight to fight inflation are also dampening the Japanese appetite for investment at present. So is the recent weakening in the yen's value against foreign currencies, which reduces pressure on Japanese exporters to cut costs by shifting output overseas.

"Given the weaker yen, China's tight money policy and the various changes in China's policies (toward foreign ventures), Japanese investment will probably slow down somewhat compared to past enthusiasm," Umeda said. "Those that fully understand the situation will keep investing. But until recently, everyone wanted to invest in China."
A recent survey of Japanese firms' overseas investment plans by daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun showed southeast Asia had replaced China as the top target in the year to March 1997.
Japanese firms were involved in 2,935 cases of investment in China in 1995, down slightly from 3,018 the previous year.

The value of Japanese investment in 1995 rose to $7.58 billion on a contract basis from $4.44 billion in 1994, but only $3.1 billion worth of the 1995 contracts was implemented, according to the Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO).
Much of the fresh money came from firms boosting existing investment rather than those setting up for the first time.
Japanese corporations are also keen to know what direction Beijing takes in its policy toward its state-owned firms, the bulk of which economists estimate are in the red.

"Depending on what policies they take to strengthen state-owned firms, their policy (toward foreign investment) could change," said Hiroshi Honkawa, assistant director of the China-North Asia section at JETRO.
"There are many uncertainties."
Japanese businesses will be watching closely to see what happens when China resumes sovereignty over Hong Kong next year as a clue to future policies, the experts said.
But they appear to have few fears about potential political upheaval following the demise of economic reform architect Deng Xiaoping, who is 92 and believed to be in frail health.
"Deng has actually already retired," said Ikegami.

"Anyway, it is not a question of who is the leader but of what the policies are, and China is unlikely to change its policy of liberalising its economy. If they want to develop their economy, they need to use foreign firms' strength -- that's what most Japanese businessmen think."
